column2: We built E from its power series. Why should adding inputs multiply outputs? Put the terms of E of x across the top, and the terms of E of y down the side. Each square contains one product. The complete grid goes on forever. We are showing its first corner, not pretending that sixteen products are the whole answer.

Instead of collecting the products by rows, collect them by total degree. Degree zero has just one square, containing one. Degree one has two squares: x and y. Their sum is x plus y. Now inspect the three squares of degree two. Before we combine them, can you recognize their sum?

They give x squared over two, plus x y, plus y squared over two. Factor out one half. Inside the brackets is x squared plus two x y plus y squared: the square of x plus y. So this diagonal contributes x plus y, squared, divided by two. The factorial in the denominator has survived.

The degree-three diagonal works the same way. In general, multiplying a degree-m diagonal by m factorial gives the binomial coefficients. The binomial theorem combines that diagonal into x plus y to the m, divided by m factorial. We have shown the complete diagonals through degree three here. Higher ones continue beyond the visible corner.

There is one analytic permission slip. Both series converge absolutely, so their product can be regrouped by diagonals without changing its sum. The diagonals are precisely the terms of E at x plus y. Therefore E of x times E of y equals E of x plus y. The multiplication law came from the factorials and convergence, not from naming the function exponential.

Set y equal to minus x. The product is E of zero, which is one, so E never vanishes. For a real x, apply the same law to two copies of half x. E of x is the square of a nonzero real number, so it is positive. Since its derivative is itself, it is increasing. Those familiar properties now follow from what we built.
